People may avoid asking questions because they fear looking stupid.
They may avoid disagreement because they fear being labeled difficult.
They may avoid apology because they fear appearing weak.
They may avoid ambition because they fear appearing arrogant.
They may avoid honesty because they fear moral judgment.
They may avoid intimacy because they fear embarrassment.
Reputation turns interaction into identity management.
When reputation is at stake, people do not only protect outcomes. They protect how they will be interpreted.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.18 Institutional Risk
Institutional risk appears when an interaction occurs inside a system with rules, records, roles, and consequences.
A school, company, court, hospital, platform, government office, or financial institution can convert speech into official action.
A casual complaint may become a report.
A statement may become evidence.
A mistake may become a record.
A diagnosis may affect treatment.
A signature may create obligation.
A performance review may shape promotion.
A disciplinary meeting may affect future access.
Institutional fields are powerful because they can preserve and act upon information.
They remember.
They classify.
They evaluate.
They punish.
They reward.
They escalate.
This is why people often behave carefully inside institutions. They know the interaction is not only interpersonal. It is procedural.
In institutional settings, the question is not only:
What does this person think of me?
It is also:
What will the system do with this information?

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.19 Social Risk and Belonging
Humans are deeply shaped by belonging.
Social risk appears when an action may affect inclusion, acceptance, loyalty, group identity, or relational stability.
In a friend group, social risk may involve being excluded.
In a family, it may involve being judged or emotionally punished.
In a workplace, it may involve being seen as not fitting the culture.
In an online community, it may involve being attacked or expelled.
In a cultural group, it may involve being labeled as betraying shared values.
Belonging pressure changes speech.
People may conform publicly while disagreeing privately.
They may laugh at jokes they dislike.
They may hide preferences.
They may perform loyalty.
They may avoid defending outsiders.
They may suppress doubt.
They may repeat group language to remain included.
Social risk is powerful because exclusion is painful.
A field does not need formal punishment if belonging itself is conditional.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.20 Asymmetry of Exposure
Exposure is often asymmetric.
One person may know more about the other than the other knows about them.
One person may be evaluated while the other evaluates.
One person may be visible while the other remains protected.
One person may have records while the other has only memory.
One person may control the platform.
One person may control the narrative.
One person may have social support.
One person may have institutional backing.
Asymmetry of exposure creates power.
A job applicant reveals qualifications, weaknesses, history, and desire for employment, while the employer reveals comparatively little.
A patient reveals bodily vulnerability, while the doctor occupies professional authority.
A student is evaluated by a teacher, while the teacher is less exposed.
A public figure is constantly visible, while anonymous audiences remain hidden.
A person sending emotional messages may become exposed if the recipient chooses to share them.
To understand risk, we must ask:
Who is more exposed?
Who controls the record?
Who can interpret whom?
Who can use the information later?
Who can walk away protected?

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
section: 4.21 The Field Can Amplify or Reduce Risk
text:
4.21 The Field Can Amplify or Reduce Risk
Situations can either amplify risk or reduce risk.
A field amplifies risk when it is public, hierarchical, punitive, ambiguous, competitive, recordable, emotionally unsafe, culturally unfamiliar, or institutionally consequential.
A field reduces risk when it is private, trusted, repairable, respectful, low-stakes, non-punitive, emotionally safe, and clear about boundaries.
For example, feedback given privately in a trusted relationship may reduce humiliation and allow learning.
The same feedback given publicly in a competitive environment may create shame and defensiveness.
A disagreement in a team with psychological safety may improve decision-making.
The same disagreement in a blame culture may damage career prospects.
A confession in a caring relationship may deepen intimacy.
The same confession in a mocking group may become a wound.
Situational design matters.
If we want honest speech, we must build fields where honesty is survivable.
If we want learning, we must build fields where mistakes are not immediately punished.
If we want trust, we must build fields where vulnerability is not exploited.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.22 Reading Stakes Before Acting
Before acting in any serious interaction, one should read the stakes.
Ask:
What matters here?
What can be gained?
What can be lost?
What can be damaged?
What can be protected?
What can become irreversible?
Who cares about the outcome?
Who has power over the consequence?
What visible issue is being discussed?
What hidden issue may actually be at stake?
Sometimes the visible topic is small, but the hidden stakes are large.
A family argument about dinner may really be about respect.
A workplace disagreement about wording may really be about authority.
A romantic conflict about timing may really be about priority.
A public debate about facts may really be about identity.
A negotiation about price may really be about trust.
Stakes are not always obvious. They must be interpreted.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.23 Reading Risk Before Speaking
After reading stakes, one must read risk.
Ask:
What can go wrong if I speak directly?
What can go wrong if I remain silent?
Who may misunderstand this?
Who may punish this?
Who may record this?
Who may benefit from misinterpreting this?
What is the worst plausible consequence?
Can the damage be repaired?
Do I have protection?
Does the other person have protection?
Is this a safe field for clarity?
Risk assessment is not cowardice. It is consequence awareness.
A person who ignores risk may call themselves honest, but they may simply be careless.
A person who sees risk clearly can still choose courage. But their courage becomes informed rather than blind.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.24 Reading Exposure Before Revealing
Before revealing something important, one must read exposure.
Ask:
What am I about to make visible?
Who will know this?
Can this information travel?
Can it be recorded?
Can it be used against me or someone else?
Is this the right person?
Is this the right time?
Is this the right medium?
Is this field capable of protecting what I reveal?
What boundary should I set around this information?
Exposure cannot always be avoided. Many meaningful interactions require it.
Trust requires some exposure.
Intimacy requires some exposure.
Leadership requires some exposure.
Learning requires some exposure.
Justice sometimes requires exposure.
But exposure should be deliberate when the stakes are high.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.25 Courage Under Risk
Risk does not mean one should avoid action.
Some situations require courage.
One may need to speak truth to power.
One may need to protect someone vulnerable.
One may need to admit fault.
One may need to challenge injustice.
One may need to set a boundary.
One may need to reveal need.
One may need to refuse harmful pressure.
One may need to act even when the field is dangerous.
Situational intelligence is not a philosophy of avoidance. It is a discipline of accurate seeing.
Courage is strongest when it understands the field.
A person who sees the risk and acts anyway is different from a person who does not see the risk at all.
The first is courageous.
The second may simply be unaware.
Risk awareness gives courage structure.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
section: 4.26 The Ethics of Creating Safer Fields
text:
4.26 The Ethics of Creating Safer Fields
This chapter has focused on reading risk. But there is also an ethical task: creating fields where unnecessary risk is reduced.
If one has power, one has responsibility for the field.
A manager can create a meeting where junior people can disagree without punishment.
A teacher can create a classroom where mistakes become learning rather than humiliation.
A parent can create a family atmosphere where children can speak without fear.
A partner can create intimacy where vulnerability is protected.
A moderator can create a public space where disagreement does not become harassment.
An institution can create procedures that reduce arbitrary punishment.
A friend can create privacy when someone is exposed.
Power is not only the ability to speak. Power is also the ability to make speech safer or more dangerous for others.
Ethical interaction asks:
Does this field protect dignity?
Does it allow repair?
Does it distribute risk fairly?
Does it punish honesty?
Does it exploit vulnerability?
Does it expose people unnecessarily?
Does it allow lower-power participants to speak?
A mature interaction system does not simply demand courage from vulnerable people. It also builds conditions where truth and dignity can survive.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.27 The Stakes-Risk-Exposure Model
A structured model of high-consequence situations can be built through three questions.








Dimension
Core Question
What It Reveals




Stakes
What can be gained, lost, damaged, or protected?
The importance of the interaction


Risk
What can go wrong, and for whom?
The possible harm or cost


Exposure
What becomes visible, recordable, or usable?
The vulnerability created by interaction



These three dimensions work together.
High stakes without high risk may create importance but not danger.
High risk without high stakes may create unnecessary anxiety.
High exposure without protection may create vulnerability.
High stakes, high risk, and high exposure together create a dangerous field.
For example, a public accusation inside a company may involve high stakes, high risk, and high exposure.
A private conversation with a trusted friend may involve emotional stakes but lower risk and controlled exposure.
A casual post online may appear low-stakes at first, but recordability can increase exposure and future risk.
The model helps us avoid vague impressions.
Instead of saying, “This feels dangerous,” we can ask:
What are the stakes?
Where is the risk?
What exposure is being created?

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.28 Common Situational Errors
People often fail because they misread stakes, risk, or exposure.
They underestimate stakes.
They think the conversation is casual when it is evaluative.
They underestimate risk.
They think direct speech will be welcomed when the hierarchy will punish it.
They underestimate exposure.
They think a message is private when it can be screenshotted.
They overestimate risk.
They treat a safe field as dangerous and become unnecessarily guarded.
They misplace urgency.
They rush because someone pressures them, not because the situation truly requires speed.
They ignore asymmetric cost.
They advise someone to “just speak up” without recognizing that the other person bears more risk.
They confuse visibility with safety.
They think being public protects people, when public visibility can also invite attack.
They confuse silence with consent.
They fail to see that silence may be risk management.
Each error comes from reading behavior without reading consequence.

title: 4  Stakes, Risk, and Exposure
text:
4.29 Conclusion: Consequence Shapes Interaction
Situations do not merely provide background. They change what action costs.
They determine what is safe, costly, urgent, or dangerous.
They affect who can speak, who must be careful, who is exposed, who is protected, who can make mistakes, who will be punished, and what can become irreversible.
This chapter establishes the third principle of situational intelligence:
Interaction must be interpreted through stakes, risk, and exposure.
A statement is not only a statement. It is an action under possible consequence.
A silence is not only absence. It may be protection, fear, calculation, discipline, or refusal.
A confession is not only honesty. It is vulnerability inside a field.
A disagreement is not only opinion. It is risk under power.
A joke is not only humor. It is meaning under audience and recordability.
A refusal is not only rejection. It is boundary under cost.
To understand human interaction, we must understand the consequence field.
Before judging speech or silence, ask:
What is at stake?
Who is at risk?
What is being exposed?
What can be repaired?
What cannot be undone?
Only then can we understand why people speak, hide, hesitate, perform, resist, or remain silent.
Human interaction happens somewhere.
And wherever it happens, something may be at stake.

title: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture
text:
A situation is not made only of visible conditions.
It is also made of expectations.
When people enter a meeting, a classroom, a dinner, a date, a family gathering, a public platform, or an institution, they do not enter as blank individuals. They bring learned assumptions about how people are supposed to behave. They know, often without explicit instruction, what can be said, what should be avoided, who should speak first, how disagreement should be expressed, how respect should be shown, how emotion should be managed, and what kind of behavior will be judged as strange, rude, professional, intimate, childish, arrogant, proper, or inappropriate.
These expectations form the normative layer of interaction.
A norm is a shared expectation about acceptable behavior.
A script is a patterned sequence of expected behavior inside a recognizable situation.
Culture is the deeper interpretive background that makes some meanings feel natural, obvious, respectful, shameful, offensive, admirable, or unacceptable.
Together, norms, scripts, and culture give situations their behavioral grammar.
They tell people how to act before anyone explains the rules.
This is why social behavior often feels intuitive to insiders and confusing to outsiders. An insider knows when to speak, when to stop, when to laugh, when to soften, when to be direct, when to show emotion, when to hide emotion, when to ask, when to wait, when to challenge, and when to remain silent. An outsider may know the words but not the field. They may understand the language but misread the expectations.
Part II studies this invisible structure.
It asks:
What expectations govern behavior inside situations?
Why do people follow patterns they rarely state explicitly?
How do norms define what is acceptable or unacceptable?
How does culture shape interpretation before conscious explanation begins?
This part moves from the immediate field of situation to the shared patterns that organize behavior within that field.
Chapter 4, Social Scripts, studies the expected patterns people follow in meetings, dates, families, workplaces, ceremonies, public life, and online spaces. It explains why many interactions unfold according to recognizable sequences, and why violating the expected sequence can create confusion, tension, or conflict.
Chapter 5, Norms and Acceptability, examines how situations define what counts as normal, appropriate, rude, professional, deviant, respectful, shameful, or excessive. It shows that acceptability is not a universal property of behavior, but a field-sensitive judgment produced by shared expectations.
Chapter 6, Culture and Interpretive Background, goes deeper into the assumptions behind norms and scripts. It studies how cultural background shapes meaning before anyone states a rule. Culture influences how people understand authority, directness, modesty, emotion, face, privacy, gender, age, hierarchy, conflict, sincerity, politeness, and responsibility.
The purpose of this part is to make implicit expectations explicit.
Many interaction failures occur because people assume their own norms are universal. They think their way of speaking is simply “clear,” while another person experiences it as rude. They think their restraint is respectful, while another person experiences it as cold. They think their informality is friendly, while another person experiences it as unprofessional. They think their direct disagreement is honest, while another person experiences it as public humiliation. They think silence means consent, while another person uses silence to preserve face or avoid escalation.
These failures are not merely personal misunderstandings. They are clashes of normative systems.
To understand interaction well, we must therefore ask:
What script is active here?
What norm is being followed or violated?
What cultural assumption is shaping interpretation?
What behavior feels natural to one side but strange to another?
What is being treated as obvious without being spoken?
Norms, scripts, and culture do not eliminate agency. People can follow them, question them, revise them, resist them, or deliberately break them. But even resistance is meaningful only because a norm exists to be resisted.
A person who refuses a script is still acting in relation to the script.
A person who breaks a norm is still acting against a recognizable expectation.
A person who challenges culture is still speaking from inside or against an inherited interpretive background.
Part II therefore establishes the second major layer of situational intelligence:
interaction = behavior inside shared expectation
To read a situation well, one must see not only the visible field, but also the invisible expectations that govern behavior within it. Norms, scripts, and culture are the hidden operating system of social life.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.1 How People Follow Expected Patterns in Meetings, Dates, Families, Workplaces, and Public Life
Human interaction is not invented from zero each time.
When people enter a meeting, a date, a family dinner, a workplace conversation, a ceremony, a classroom, a negotiation, or a public event, they usually do not need to ask, “What happens next?” They already carry a rough expectation of how the interaction should unfold.
People know that a meeting usually begins with opening remarks or agenda-setting.
They know that a first date usually involves greeting, small talk, mutual discovery, impression management, and gradual testing of comfort.
They know that a family dinner may involve greetings, food, care, questions, generational roles, indirect pressure, and emotional history.
They know that a workplace update usually requires concision, relevance, status awareness, and progress reporting.
They know that a public ceremony requires respect for sequence, role, symbolic order, and audience expectation.
These patterns are social scripts.
A social script is an expected pattern of behavior inside a recognizable situation.
It tells people what usually happens, in what order, with what tone, under what role expectations, and with what boundaries.
Scripts make interaction easier because people do not need to negotiate every detail from scratch. But scripts also constrain behavior because they define what counts as normal, strange, respectful, rude, sincere, professional, childish, intimate, excessive, or inappropriate.
To understand interaction, we must understand scripts.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.2 What Is a Social Script?
A social script is a learned structure for action.
It answers:
What kind of situation is this?
Who plays what role?
What happens first?
What happens next?
What language is expected?
What emotion is appropriate?
What topics are allowed?
What behavior would violate the field?
How should the interaction end?
A script does not need to be written down. Most scripts are learned through repetition, observation, correction, embarrassment, imitation, reward, and punishment.
Children learn scripts by watching adults.
Employees learn workplace scripts by observing meetings.
Students learn classroom scripts by repeated participation.
Friends learn friendship scripts through shared habits.
Couples build private scripts through repeated emotional exchanges.
Citizens learn public scripts through institutions, media, ceremonies, and rules.
Online users learn platform scripts through likes, comments, screenshots, trends, ridicule, and algorithmic reward.
Scripts are therefore social memory.
They preserve what a group has learned to expect from a situation.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.3 Scripts Reduce Uncertainty
One function of scripts is to reduce uncertainty.
Without scripts, every interaction would require constant negotiation.
Should I speak first?
Should I shake hands?
Should I ask personal questions?
Should I be formal?
Should I make eye contact?
Should I give reasons?
Should I wait?
Should I challenge?
Should I apologize?
Should I leave?
Scripts provide default answers.
In a restaurant, one does not need to invent the interaction with the waiter from the beginning. There is a known sequence: enter, be seated, receive menu, order, eat, pay, leave.
In a job interview, both interviewer and candidate know the broad structure: greeting, introduction, questions, self-presentation, evaluation, candidate questions, closing.
In a classroom, students know that the teacher usually organizes the lesson, asks questions, evaluates answers, and controls the pace.
In a wedding, participants know that the occasion is symbolic, formal, emotional, and sequence-bound.
The script does not determine every detail, but it gives the interaction a recognizable path.
This is why scripts create comfort. People feel safer when they know what kind of situation they are in and what is expected from them.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.4 Scripts Also Create Constraint
Scripts reduce uncertainty, but they also create constraint.
Once a script is active, deviation becomes meaningful.
If someone refuses to greet others at a dinner, the refusal may be interpreted as coldness, hostility, arrogance, or emotional withdrawal.
If someone turns a casual hangout into a serious interrogation, the script is violated.
If someone treats a job interview like a therapy session, the script is violated.
If someone treats a funeral like a party, the script is violated.
If someone treats a private friendship conversation like a public debate, the script is violated.
If someone treats a public ceremony like an informal joke, the script is violated.
A script creates expectations. When behavior breaks those expectations, people do not see only behavior. They see the violation of a field.
This is why social failure often feels larger than the action itself. The person did not merely say something unusual. They disrupted the expected order of the situation.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.5 The Structure of a Script
A social script usually contains several components.







Component
Question




Situation type
What kind of interaction is this?


Roles
Who is expected to do what?


Sequence
What usually happens first, next, and last?


Tone
What emotional style is appropriate?


Topics
What can be discussed, and what should be avoided?


Boundaries
What would be too much, too soon, too direct, or too distant?


Signals
What gestures, phrases, or behaviors show cooperation?


Exit
How does the interaction properly end?



For example, the script of a first meeting may include greeting, self-introduction, polite distance, limited personal disclosure, basic curiosity, and a clean exit.
The script of a performance review may include formal tone, evidence, evaluation, self-defense, future goals, and controlled emotion.
The script of a family reunion may include greeting elders, eating together, asking about life, exchanging care, managing sensitive topics, and maintaining family face.
The script of an online debate may include positioning, evidence, counterargument, audience signaling, and status defense.
Each script organizes not only what people do, but also how people interpret what others do.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.6 Meeting Scripts
Meetings are among the most common scripted interactions in modern institutional life.
A meeting usually carries expectations about purpose, turn-taking, relevance, role, time, and decision.
A basic meeting script may include:
opening;
agenda-setting;
updates;
discussion;
clarification;
decision;
assignment;
closing.
Even when no one explicitly announces the script, participants sense it. They know that rambling may be judged negatively. They know that speaking too much may signal poor judgment. They know that silence may be interpreted as agreement, disengagement, resistance, or caution depending on the field. They know that disagreement must often be framed carefully, especially under hierarchy.
A meeting is not only a discussion. It is a structured field of visibility.
People perform competence.
They show alignment.
They protect status.
They manage disagreement.
They signal responsibility.
They avoid unnecessary exposure.
In some organizations, the meeting script rewards clarity and challenge.
In others, it rewards agreement and face protection.
In some meetings, junior participants are expected to speak.
In others, they are expected to wait.
In some meetings, disagreement is productive.
In others, disagreement is politically dangerous.
The visible script may be “discussion,” but the hidden script may be “show loyalty,” “avoid blame,” “protect leadership,” “compete for influence,” or “create a record.”
Situational intelligence requires reading both the official meeting script and the real meeting script.

title: 5  Social Scripts

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.8 Family Scripts
Family interaction is heavily scripted, but often in ways that are difficult to see from inside.
A family script defines roles, obligations, emotional patterns, acceptable speech, authority relations, conflict styles, care expectations, and boundaries of belonging.
In many families, scripts answer questions such as:
Who speaks for the family?
Who must obey?
Who is allowed to be angry?
Who must keep harmony?
Who is responsible for care?
Who is allowed to leave?
Who must explain themselves?
Who can criticize?
Who cannot be criticized?
Who is treated as successful, difficult, fragile, selfish, irresponsible, or favored?
Family scripts are powerful because they are learned early and repeated for years.
A person may become “the responsible one,” “the rebellious one,” “the silent one,” “the successful one,” “the emotional one,” “the problem child,” “the mediator,” “the caretaker,” or “the outsider.”
Once a role is scripted, the family may keep interpreting the person through that role even after they change.
Family scripts often appear during repeated situations: meals, holidays, money conversations, marriage discussions, caregiving, education choices, career decisions, inheritance, conflict, illness, and crisis.
For example, a family dinner may officially be about eating together, but the deeper script may include hierarchy, concern, comparison, pressure, guilt, affection, control, and belonging.
A parent asking, “How is your work?” may not be asking for neutral information. Inside a family script, the question may carry expectation, judgment, worry, comparison, or pressure.
A child saying, “I’m fine,” may not be giving information. They may be managing exposure.
Family scripts are difficult because they mix love and control, care and pressure, memory and expectation.
To understand family interaction, one must ask:
What role is this person being pulled into?
What old script is being repeated?
What topics activate the family system?
What behavior is rewarded?
What behavior is punished?
What truth cannot be spoken directly?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.9 Workplace Scripts
Workplaces are dense script environments.
They contain official scripts and unofficial scripts.
Official workplace scripts include hiring, onboarding, reporting, collaboration, meetings, performance review, promotion, resignation, conflict resolution, and leadership communication.
Unofficial workplace scripts include status games, loyalty signaling, impression management, blame avoidance, political alignment, emotional control, and informal networking.
A workplace may officially say, “We value open communication.”
But the real script may say, “Do not challenge senior leadership in public.”
A company may officially say, “Mistakes are learning opportunities.”
But the real script may say, “Never be the person visibly responsible for failure.”
A team may officially say, “Everyone’s opinion matters.”
But the real script may say, “Only certain people’s opinions influence decisions.”
A manager may officially ask for feedback.
But the real script may make feedback risky.
This gap between official script and real script is crucial.
Many people fail in workplaces because they follow the official script while ignoring the hidden script. They speak honestly when the field only wanted symbolic participation. They challenge a decision when the decision was already made. They ask for fairness when the real script is loyalty. They expect process when the real script is power.
This does not mean one should simply submit to hidden scripts. But one must see them.
To act intelligently in a workplace, one must distinguish:
What is officially said?
What is actually rewarded?
What is punished?
Who is allowed to break rules?
Who must follow them?
What kind of disagreement is safe?
What kind of disagreement is remembered?
Workplace maturity requires script literacy.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.10 Public Life Scripts
Public life is also scripted.
People behave differently in public because public fields contain audience, visibility, reputation, symbolic meaning, and collective judgment.
Public scripts govern ceremonies, speeches, protests, debates, interviews, service encounters, public apologies, platform posts, official announcements, and civic behavior.
In public, people often speak not only to the immediate listener, but to an observing audience.
This creates performance.
A politician answering a question may not primarily answer the questioner. They may speak to voters, media, allies, donors, opponents, and history.
A public apology may not only express regret. It may manage reputation, satisfy institutional demand, signal accountability, reduce damage, or perform humility.
A public disagreement may not only resolve a factual issue. It may display courage, loyalty, moral position, group identity, or dominance.
A platform post may not only share thought. It may signal taste, status, belonging, ideology, competence, desirability, or virtue.
Public scripts are powerful because they reward legibility.
People learn what kinds of performance receive attention.
They learn what can be praised, attacked, mocked, amplified, or punished.
They learn that public fields often simplify complex realities into visible positions.
This is why public life can distort interaction. It encourages people to speak in ways that are audience-readable, morally clear, emotionally intense, and socially rewarding, even when private understanding would require nuance.
Public scripts do not eliminate sincerity, but they reshape sincerity through performance.

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.11 Script Fit and Script Misfit
A person fits a script when their behavior matches the expected pattern of the situation.
A person misfits a script when their behavior violates the pattern.
Script fit can create smooth interaction.
Script misfit can create discomfort, confusion, tension, embarrassment, or conflict.
For example:
A person gives a long personal confession during a short work update.
A person jokes during a solemn moment.
A person negotiates aggressively during a friendly dinner.
A person treats a first date like a job interview.
A person treats a job interview like casual friendship.
A person gives direct criticism in a culture where criticism must be indirect.
A person speaks as an equal in a hierarchy that expects deference.
A person uses institutional language in an intimate relationship.
In each case, the problem is not only the content. The problem is the mismatch between behavior and script.
Script misfit is one of the most common sources of social failure.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.12 Scripts and Power
Scripts are not neutral.
They often protect power.
A script may define who speaks first, who interrupts, who explains, who apologizes, who serves, who listens, who sacrifices, and who receives credit.
In a hierarchy, the script may require lower-status participants to be polite, patient, indirect, and self-controlled, while higher-status participants can be direct, emotional, dismissive, or demanding.
In a family, the script may require younger members to show respect while elders can criticize without equal accountability.
In a workplace, the script may require employees to show enthusiasm even when they are exhausted.
In public life, the script may require certain people to remain calm under provocation, while others are allowed anger.
In gendered situations, scripts may define who initiates, who cares, who waits, who softens, who performs confidence, who performs modesty, and who absorbs emotional labor.
To analyze scripts seriously, we must ask:
Who benefits from this script?
Who carries the burden?
Who is made visible?
Who is silenced?
Who is protected?
Who is exposed?
Who can break the script without punishment?
Who is punished for breaking it?
Scripts organize behavior, but they also distribute power.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.13 Scripts and Identity
Scripts do not only shape external behavior. They shape identity.
When a person repeatedly plays a role, the role can become part of how they understand themselves.
A child who is always treated as irresponsible may begin to expect failure.
A worker who is always positioned as support may stop imagining leadership.
A person repeatedly praised for being strong may lose permission to show need.
A person repeatedly scripted as attractive may learn to perform desirability.
A person repeatedly scripted as difficult may become defensive before they are attacked.
A person repeatedly scripted as smart may fear mistakes because mistakes threaten identity.
Scripts can become internalized.
The external expectation becomes an inner voice.
This is why changing behavior is often difficult. A person is not only changing action. They may be leaving a familiar script.
To leave a script can feel like betrayal, arrogance, danger, loneliness, or loss of identity.
A person who stops being the family mediator may be accused of selfishness.
A person who stops pleasing others may be called cold.
A person who stops performing competence may feel exposed.
A person who stops obeying hierarchy may be called disrespectful.
Script change often creates resistance because systems prefer familiar roles.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.14 Scripts and Emotional Labor
Many scripts assign emotional labor unevenly.
Emotional labor means managing one’s own emotion and often managing the emotion of others to keep the interaction functioning.
In some family scripts, one person must keep peace.
In some workplace scripts, service workers must remain pleasant regardless of customer behavior.
In some gender scripts, women may be expected to soften conflict, remember emotional details, and maintain relational harmony.
In some leadership scripts, leaders must project confidence even under uncertainty.
In some friendship scripts, one person becomes the listener while rarely being listened to.
In some public scripts, marginalized people may be expected to explain calmly even when being disrespected.
Emotional labor can be caring and meaningful when freely chosen.
But it becomes exploitative when one person is repeatedly required to absorb tension, soften truth, protect others’ feelings, and remain acceptable while others behave freely.
Script analysis therefore asks:
Who must regulate emotion here?
Who is allowed to express emotion?
Who must make others comfortable?
Who receives care?
Who provides care?
Who pays the emotional cost of keeping the script stable?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.15 Script Ambiguity
Not every situation has a clear script.
Modern life often produces ambiguous scripts.
Is this dinner a date or a friendly meeting?
Is this meeting a real discussion or a decision announcement?
Is this apology personal or performative?
Is this message private or semi-public?
Is this online space casual or professional?
Is this workplace relationship friendly or hierarchical?
Is this family advice care or control?
Is this invitation social, romantic, strategic, or obligatory?
Ambiguous scripts create anxiety because people do not know which expectations apply.
When scripts are ambiguous, people often test the field.
They use small signals.
They ask indirect questions.
They watch reactions.
They reveal gradually.
They imitate the other person’s tone.
They wait for role clarification.
They choose reversible language.
They avoid strong commitment.
Ambiguity is not always bad. It can allow flexibility, creativity, and gradual negotiation. But if ambiguity is unmanaged, it can produce misreading, disappointment, embarrassment, manipulation, or conflict.
Situational intelligence includes the ability to clarify scripts without damaging the field.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.16 Script Shifts
An interaction may begin under one script and then shift into another.
A casual conversation becomes a serious confrontation.
A friendly meeting becomes an evaluation.
A joke becomes an insult.
A private disagreement becomes a public conflict.
A brainstorming session becomes a decision meeting.
A date becomes a negotiation of boundaries.
A family dinner becomes a life audit.
A customer service interaction becomes a moral dispute.
A text conversation becomes evidence.
Script shifts are dangerous because participants may not shift at the same time.
One person may still think the interaction is playful, while another has become serious.
One person may think they are exploring, while another thinks a decision is being made.
One person may think the conversation is private, while another treats it as recordable.
One person may think they are giving advice, while another experiences judgment.
Many conflicts begin when people operate under different scripts inside the same interaction.
A skilled person notices when the script has shifted.
They may say:
“Are we discussing this casually, or are we making a decision?”
“Do you want advice, or do you want me to listen?”
“Is this feedback, or is this a formal evaluation?”
“Should we talk about this privately?”
“Are we joking, or is this serious?”
Such questions are not merely communication tools. They are script-repair tools.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.17 Script Violation
A script violation occurs when someone breaks expected behavior.
Script violation can be destructive, but it can also be necessary.
Some violations are careless.
A person interrupts a ceremony for attention.
A person humiliates someone publicly.
A person uses intimate information in a professional field.
A person ignores boundaries.
A person refuses basic respect.
These violations damage trust because they disrupt the field without ethical purpose.
Other violations are courageous or transformative.
A person refuses a harmful family role.
A junior employee names a hidden problem.
A citizen challenges an unjust public script.
A victim refuses silence.
A marginalized person rejects a degrading expectation.
A leader breaks a blame script and protects others.
A teacher changes a classroom script from fear to learning.
Not all script-breaking is wrong.
The question is:
What script is being broken?
Why is it being broken?
Who benefits from the script?
Who is harmed by it?
What risk does the violation create?
What new field is being opened?
A mature theory of interaction must distinguish between destructive misfit and necessary refusal.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.19 Learning Scripts
People learn scripts through participation.
They observe.
They imitate.
They are corrected.
They experience embarrassment.
They notice what gets rewarded.
They notice what gets punished.
They adjust.
Some scripts are learned explicitly: school rules, professional procedures, legal forms, ceremonial instructions.
Other scripts are learned implicitly: how to read family tension, how to behave around authority, how to show respect, how to disagree politely, how to signal attraction, how to avoid shame, how to perform belonging.
A person moving across class, culture, industry, institution, or country may experience script shock.
They may be intelligent and capable, but still misread the field because the script is unfamiliar.
This is especially important in social mobility.
Changing environments often requires learning new scripts: academic scripts, professional scripts, elite scripts, bureaucratic scripts, networking scripts, public speech scripts, institutional writing scripts, and digital self-presentation scripts.
A person may fail not because they lack ability, but because they have not yet learned the script of the new field.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.20 Scripts and Social Mobility
Social mobility is partly script mobility.
To enter a new world, one must learn how that world organizes interaction.
A person entering university must learn academic scripts: discussion, citation, argument, office hours, research language, intellectual disagreement.
A person entering a corporate environment must learn workplace scripts: meetings, status updates, stakeholder management, email tone, performance review, promotion talk.
A person entering elite social spaces must learn scripts of taste, restraint, confidence, indirect signaling, and network behavior.
A person entering public intellectual life must learn scripts of argument, positioning, credibility, audience, and reputation.
A person entering entrepreneurship must learn scripts of pitching, negotiation, risk framing, investor language, hiring, and market storytelling.
These scripts are not merely superficial manners. They are access structures.
People who know the script can move more easily.
People who do not know the script may be judged as unprofessional, immature, rude, weak, arrogant, or unsuitable, even when they have real competence.
This is why making scripts explicit can be emancipatory. It gives people access to fields that otherwise hide their rules.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.21 Script Awareness and Freedom
The goal of script analysis is not blind conformity.
The goal is freedom through awareness.
A person who does not see scripts is controlled by them unconsciously.
A person who sees scripts can choose.
They can follow a script when it serves dignity, clarity, safety, or coordination.
They can bend a script when adaptation is needed.
They can refuse a script when it is unjust, harmful, degrading, or false.
They can create a new script when the old one no longer fits.
Script awareness gives action more precision.
It helps a person know when to be formal and when to be warm.
When to follow procedure and when to humanize the field.
When to speak directly and when to protect face.
When to remain silent and when silence becomes complicity.
When to respect tradition and when tradition becomes control.
When to perform competence and when to reveal uncertainty.
When to preserve harmony and when harmony hides harm.
Scripts should not be masters. They should be readable structures.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.22 The Social Script Model
A structured model of social scripts can be built through the following questions:







Dimension
Guiding Question




Situation type
What kind of interaction is this?


Expected sequence
What usually happens first, next, and last?


Roles
Who is expected to lead, follow, listen, speak, serve, judge, or decide?


Tone
What emotional style is expected?


Permission
What can be said or done here?


Boundary
What would be too direct, too personal, too public, too emotional, or too informal?


Hidden rule
What is expected but not openly stated?


Power distribution
Who benefits from the script, and who carries the burden?


Violation cost
What happens if someone breaks the script?


Repair path
How can mismatch be corrected?



This model helps convert vague social intuition into explicit analysis.
Instead of saying, “This feels wrong,” we can ask:
Which script is being violated?
Instead of saying, “This person is awkward,” we can ask:
Are they unfamiliar with this field’s script?
Instead of saying, “This person is disrespectful,” we can ask:
Did they violate a norm of role, timing, tone, audience, or boundary?
Instead of saying, “This person is fake,” we can ask:
Are they performing the script required by the situation?
Script analysis makes interaction more intelligible.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.23 Common Script Errors
Several errors appear repeatedly in human interaction.
The first is using the wrong script.
A person uses a friendship script in a professional setting, or a professional script in an intimate relationship.
The second is missing the hidden script.
A person follows the official rule but fails to notice the informal expectation.
The third is assuming one’s own script is universal.
A person believes their cultural, family, class, or workplace script is simply “normal.”
The fourth is failing to notice script shift.
A conversation changes from casual to serious, but the person continues joking.
The fifth is confusing script performance with inner truth.
A person behaves formally in a formal field, and others assume they are emotionally cold.
The sixth is treating script compliance as moral goodness.
A person follows expected behavior, but the script itself may be harmful.
The seventh is treating script violation as automatically wrong.
A person breaks a script, but the violation may be necessary to expose injustice or create change.
These errors show why scripts must be read carefully, not mechanically.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 5  Social Scripts
text:
5.24 Conclusion: Interaction Has Expected Patterns
Social life is patterned.
People do not enter every interaction empty-handed. They carry scripts: learned expectations about what kind of situation this is, what roles are active, what sequence should unfold, what tone is appropriate, what boundaries exist, and what behavior will be accepted or punished.
Scripts make interaction possible by reducing uncertainty.
They also constrain interaction by defining normality.
They can coordinate behavior.
They can protect dignity.
They can preserve order.
They can hide power.
They can assign emotional labor.
They can trap people in roles.
They can be followed, bent, repaired, refused, or rewritten.
This chapter establishes the fourth principle of situational intelligence:
Human interaction is guided by social scripts.
To understand behavior, we must ask not only what a person did, but what script they were following, violating, resisting, or trying to create.
A meeting is not only a discussion.
A date is not only conversation.
A family dinner is not only eating.
A workplace interaction is not only information exchange.
A public event is not only visible action.
Each is a scripted field.
To read interaction well, we must learn to read the script.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.1 How Situations Define What Is Normal, Appropriate, Rude, Professional, or Deviant
Every situation contains standards.
These standards may be spoken or unspoken, formal or informal, strict or flexible, moral or practical, visible or hidden. They tell people what counts as normal, acceptable, appropriate, respectful, rude, professional, childish, excessive, strange, offensive, deviant, or dangerous.
People rarely enter an interaction by asking, “What is the norm here?” Yet they constantly act under norms.
They decide how loudly to speak.
They decide how much emotion to show.
They decide how direct to be.
They decide how much personal information to reveal.
They decide whether to challenge, agree, laugh, apologize, refuse, or remain silent.
They decide whether something is “too much,” “not enough,” “out of place,” “unprofessional,” “disrespectful,” “cold,” “fake,” “immature,” “serious,” “normal,” or “weird.”
These judgments are not produced by behavior alone. They are produced by behavior inside a field of norms.
A norm is a shared expectation about what behavior is acceptable in a given situation.
Norms are powerful because they often appear natural. People do not usually experience their own norms as local rules. They experience them as obvious reality.
They say:
“That’s rude.”
“That’s inappropriate.”
“That’s normal.”
“That’s unprofessional.”
“That’s too much.”
“That’s just how things are done.”
But behind each judgment is a field.
The central question of this chapter is:
How do situations define what counts as acceptable behavior?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.2 Norms Are Situational Standards
A norm is not merely a personal preference.
A preference says, “I like this.”
A norm says, “This is how people are supposed to behave here.”
This difference matters.
If someone says, “I prefer quiet conversation,” they are expressing a preference.
If someone says, “You should not speak loudly in this place,” they are invoking a norm.
Norms create shared standards. They allow people to coordinate behavior without negotiating everything explicitly.
In a library, quietness is expected.
In a concert, loudness may be acceptable.
In a classroom, asking questions may be encouraged.
In a courtroom, speaking out of turn may be punished.
In a close friendship, emotional honesty may be welcome.
In a formal workplace meeting, the same emotional intensity may be judged as inappropriate.
In a family, direct refusal may be seen as disrespect.
In a professional negotiation, direct refusal may be seen as clarity.
The behavior is not interpreted alone. It is interpreted against a norm.
This is why acceptability is field-sensitive.
The same action can be acceptable in one field and unacceptable in another.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.3 Normal Is Not Universal
People often confuse “normal” with “universal.”
But normality is produced by a field.
What feels normal in one family may feel controlling in another.
What feels normal in one workplace may feel cold in another.
What feels normal in one culture may feel rude in another.
What feels normal in one social class may feel excessive, arrogant, or insecure in another.
What feels normal online may feel aggressive face-to-face.
What feels normal among close friends may feel invasive among acquaintances.
Normality is not simply what most humans naturally do. It is what a specific group, setting, culture, institution, or relationship has learned to expect.
This is why people may experience shock when they enter a new field.
A person from an indirect communication culture may find direct disagreement rude.
A person from a direct communication culture may find indirectness confusing or dishonest.
A person from a formal institution may find casual workplaces chaotic.
A person from an informal environment may find formal institutions stiff and artificial.
A person from a high-control family may find open disagreement dangerous.
A person from a dialogic family may find silence unhealthy.
Each person carries a different map of normal.
Situational intelligence begins when we stop asking only, “Is this normal?” and begin asking:
Normal according to which field?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
section: 6.4 Appropriateness: Fit Between Behavior and Field
text:
6.4 Appropriateness: Fit Between Behavior and Field
Appropriateness is the fit between behavior and situation.
An action is appropriate when it matches the active field: its occasion, roles, tone, stakes, audience, hierarchy, and symbolic meaning.
An action is inappropriate when it violates that fit.
Appropriateness does not mean moral goodness in the deepest sense. Something can be appropriate but morally empty. Something can be inappropriate but ethically necessary.
For example, polite silence may be appropriate in a formal ceremony.
But if the ceremony hides injustice, breaking silence may be morally necessary.
A manager’s calm tone may be professionally appropriate.
But if the calm tone hides cruelty, appropriateness becomes a mask.
A child’s obedience may be culturally appropriate.
But if obedience destroys selfhood, the norm becomes harmful.
Therefore, appropriateness must be understood carefully.
It is a situational judgment, not an ultimate moral judgment.
It asks:
Does this behavior fit this field?
But a deeper ethical question must also ask:
Is this field itself just?
Norms define fit. Ethics evaluates the norm.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.5 Rudeness: Violation of Expected Respect
Rudeness is often a norm violation involving respect.
A behavior is judged rude when it seems to ignore, insult, expose, dismiss, interrupt, pressure, embarrass, or disrespect another person according to the standards of the situation.
But rudeness is not always obvious.
Direct criticism may be rude in one field and necessary in another.
Interrupting may be rude in a formal conversation but acceptable in a fast-moving creative discussion.
Asking about salary may be rude in one culture and normal in another.
Not greeting elders may be rude in one family system and insignificant in another.
Refusing food may be rude in one setting and ordinary in another.
Looking someone in the eye may signal respect in one culture and disrespect in another.
Avoiding eye contact may signal respect in one field and dishonesty in another.
Rudeness is therefore not merely located in the action. It is located in the relation between action and norm.
When people argue about rudeness, they are often arguing about which norm should govern the field.
One person says, “I was just being honest.”
Another says, “You humiliated me.”
One person says, “I was only joking.”
Another says, “That was disrespectful.”
One person says, “I asked a simple question.”
Another says, “That question crossed a boundary.”
The conflict is not only about intention. It is about acceptability.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.6 Professionalism: Norms of Institutional Behavior
Professionalism is a norm system for behavior inside work and institutional fields.
It defines how people are expected to speak, dress, respond, decide, disagree, handle emotion, manage time, respect roles, protect records, and represent responsibility.
Professionalism often includes:
clarity;
reliability;
role awareness;
boundary control;
emotional restraint;
respectful communication;
procedural discipline;
accountability;
competence signaling;
attention to consequence.
In a professional field, behavior is not judged only by personal sincerity. It is judged by whether it supports the functioning of the institution.
A person may feel angry, but professionalism may require controlled expression.
A person may dislike a colleague, but professionalism may require cooperation.
A person may want to speak casually, but professionalism may require precision.
A person may want to avoid conflict, but professionalism may require naming the problem.
A person may want to be fully authentic, but professionalism may require separating private emotion from public role.
Professionalism can protect fairness, clarity, and dignity.
But it can also become a tool of suppression.
Sometimes “be professional” means “communicate clearly and responsibly.”
Sometimes it means “do not expose power.”
Sometimes it means “hide your pain.”
Sometimes it means “accept mistreatment quietly.”
Sometimes it means “perform emotional control while others violate you.”
Therefore, professionalism must be analyzed as a norm, not worshiped as an absolute virtue.
The question is:
What behavior does this field call professional?
Who defines professionalism here?
Who benefits from that definition?
Whose emotion is labeled unprofessional?
Whose aggression is labeled leadership?
Whose silence is labeled maturity?
Whose honesty is labeled disruption?
Professionalism is not neutral. It distributes permission.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
section: 6.7 Deviance: Behavior Outside the Accepted Range
text:
6.7 Deviance: Behavior Outside the Accepted Range
Deviance is behavior that falls outside the accepted range of a norm system.
A deviant action is not necessarily immoral. It is behavior that a group, institution, or culture marks as abnormal, unacceptable, threatening, shameful, ridiculous, or punishable.
Deviance can be destructive.
A person may violate consent, break trust, abuse power, humiliate others, or ignore basic dignity.
But deviance can also be creative, courageous, or liberating.
A person may reject a harmful family role.
A worker may expose corruption.
A citizen may challenge unjust law.
An artist may break aesthetic convention.
A thinker may question inherited belief.
A child may refuse a script of obedience.
A marginalized person may reject a degrading expectation.
Norm systems often label necessary change as deviance before later recognizing it as progress.
Therefore, we must distinguish between two kinds of deviance:
destructive deviance, which damages dignity, safety, trust, or justice;
transformative deviance, which violates an existing norm in order to create a better field.
A serious theory of interaction cannot treat all deviance as bad.
It must ask:
What norm is being violated?
Why does the norm exist?
Whom does it protect?
Whom does it control?
What harm does the violation create?
What possibility does the violation open?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
section: 6.8 Norms Are Often Invisible Until Broken
text:
6.8 Norms Are Often Invisible Until Broken
Norms usually become visible when someone violates them.
People may not notice the norm of quietness until someone speaks loudly.
They may not notice the norm of punctuality until someone arrives late.
They may not notice the norm of emotional restraint until someone cries.
They may not notice the norm of hierarchy until someone challenges authority.
They may not notice the norm of privacy until someone reveals personal information publicly.
They may not notice the norm of politeness until someone refuses greeting.
They may not notice the norm of deference until someone speaks as an equal.
Norms are like the grammar of social life. When followed, they disappear into the background. When broken, they become visible.
This is why norm violations often produce strong reactions.
People are not only responding to the specific act. They are responding to the disturbance of the field.
A late arrival may not merely be about time. It may be read as disrespect.
A public disagreement may not merely be about opinion. It may be read as challenge.
A direct refusal may not merely be about preference. It may be read as rebellion.
A personal question may not merely be curiosity. It may be read as invasion.
A joke may not merely be humor. It may be read as boundary violation.
The field reacts because its expected order has been disturbed.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.9 Norms Create Predictability
Norms help people predict one another.
They reduce uncertainty by providing behavioral expectations.
When people share norms, they can coordinate smoothly.
They know how to greet.
They know how to apologize.
They know how to show respect.
They know how to disagree.
They know how to ask for help.
They know how to leave.
They know how much emotion to show.
They know when a conversation is over.
They know what counts as too direct, too distant, too personal, too slow, too intense, or too casual.
This predictability reduces social friction.
It allows groups to function without endless explanation.
In this sense, norms are not merely oppressive. They are also enabling structures.
Without norms, people would constantly misunderstand one another.
Every interaction would require negotiation from zero.
Shared norms allow social life to move.
The problem is not that norms exist. The problem is that norms can become rigid, hidden, unequal, outdated, or unjust.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.10 Norms Create Judgment
Norms do not only coordinate. They judge.
They produce approval and disapproval.
They tell people who is polite, rude, mature, childish, professional, unstable, respectable, shameful, normal, strange, civilized, backward, confident, arrogant, humble, weak, loyal, selfish, sincere, fake, disciplined, or deviant.
These judgments shape identity.
A person repeatedly judged through a norm may begin to internalize that judgment.
A quiet child may be called obedient in one family and passive in another.
A direct woman may be called confident in one field and aggressive in another.
An emotional man may be called authentic in one setting and weak in another.
An ambitious student may be praised in one culture and seen as arrogant in another.
A person who protects boundaries may be called healthy in one field and selfish in another.
Norms do not merely evaluate behavior. They produce social labels.
These labels can open or close possibility.
They can give dignity or remove it.
They can make a person feel legitimate or defective.
This is why norm analysis is not trivial. Norms participate in the making of social reality.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.11 Norms and Sanctions
A norm is supported by sanctions.
A sanction is a response that rewards norm-following or punishes norm-violation.
Sanctions can be formal or informal.
Formal sanctions include legal penalties, school discipline, workplace warnings, platform bans, institutional rejection, fines, demotion, dismissal, or official records.
Informal sanctions include embarrassment, gossip, exclusion, criticism, silence, ridicule, loss of trust, withdrawal of affection, status reduction, coldness, mockery, or moral judgment.
Informal sanctions are often more powerful than formal rules.
A family may not have written rules, but emotional punishment may strongly enforce obedience.
A workplace may claim openness, but reputational punishment may prevent dissent.
A friend group may have no formal authority, but exclusion can discipline behavior.
An online community may rely on mockery, pile-ons, or loss of visibility.
Sanctions teach people what the norm really is.
Do not only listen to what a group says it values.
Watch what it rewards.
Watch what it punishes.
A field’s true norms are revealed by its sanctions.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.12 Official Norms and Real Norms
Many fields have a gap between official norms and real norms.
Official norms are what the group claims to value.
Real norms are what the group actually rewards and punishes.
A company may officially value innovation, but punish risk.
A school may officially value curiosity, but reward obedience.
A family may officially value honesty, but punish uncomfortable truth.
A public platform may officially value dialogue, but reward outrage.
A team may officially value collaboration, but reward individual credit-taking.
A culture may officially value humility, but reward status display.
An institution may officially value fairness, but protect insiders.
This gap is one of the most important things to read in any field.
If a person follows official norms while ignoring real norms, they may be confused by the consequences.
They say, “But they told me to speak honestly.”
Yet honesty was punished.
They say, “But they said mistakes are okay.”
Yet mistakes damaged their reputation.
They say, “But they said everyone is equal.”
Yet hierarchy controlled the outcome.
They say, “But they said they wanted feedback.”
Yet feedback was treated as disloyalty.
Situational intelligence requires distinguishing declared values from operative norms.
The field is not defined by slogans. It is defined by consequence.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.13 Norms and Power
Norms are never separate from power.
Power influences which norms become dominant, whose behavior is judged, whose behavior is excused, and whose comfort defines acceptability.
High-status people often have more freedom to violate norms.
Low-status people often bear heavier consequences.
A senior leader may speak harshly and be called decisive.
A junior employee may speak similarly and be called disrespectful.
A wealthy person may dress casually and be called relaxed.
A poor person may dress casually and be judged unprofessional.
A powerful person may be emotional and be seen as passionate.
A less protected person may be emotional and be seen as unstable.
A dominant group may define its own style as neutral and others’ styles as excessive, foreign, rude, or improper.
Norms can therefore disguise power as manners.
They can make hierarchy look like etiquette.
They can make exclusion look like standards.
They can make obedience look like respect.
They can make silence look like maturity.
They can make conformity look like professionalism.
This does not mean all norms are oppressive. It means every norm must be read with the question of power.
Who defines this norm?
Who is judged by it?
Who is exempt from it?
Who must adapt?
Who pays the cost of compliance?
Who gains legitimacy from it?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.14 Norms and Face
Many norms protect face.
Face means a person’s social dignity, image, and claim to respect within a field.
In many interactions, people do not only exchange information. They manage face.
They avoid embarrassing others.
They soften criticism.
They give indirect refusal.
They praise publicly and criticize privately.
They allow someone to retreat without humiliation.
They use polite forms to preserve dignity.
They pretend not to notice minor mistakes.
Norms of face can protect social harmony and human dignity.
But face norms can also hide truth.
They can prevent necessary criticism.
They can protect powerful people from accountability.
They can make victims preserve the dignity of those who harmed them.
They can turn honesty into rudeness.
They can turn silence into moral expectation.
Therefore, face norms are double-edged.
They can humanize interaction.
They can also suppress reality.
Situational intelligence asks:
Whose face is being protected?
At what cost?
Is face protecting dignity or hiding harm?
Is directness necessary here, or would it create needless humiliation?
Is indirectness respectful, or is it avoiding responsibility?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.15 Norms and Emotion
Every field has emotional norms.
These norms define which emotions may be shown, by whom, in what form, and with what consequence.
In some families, anger is permitted but sadness is mocked.
In some workplaces, confidence is expected and uncertainty is hidden.
In some cultures, grief must be expressed visibly.
In others, grief must be restrained.
In some friendships, vulnerability is welcome.
In others, humor replaces emotional disclosure.
In public debate, anger may be rewarded if it signals moral force.
In court, emotional control may be required to maintain procedural credibility.
Emotional norms shape how people appear.
A person may seem cold because the field punishes vulnerability.
A person may seem agreeable because the field punishes anger.
A person may seem dramatic because their emotional style comes from another norm system.
A person may seem strong because they have learned never to show need.
A person may seem calm not because they are unhurt, but because the situation does not permit visible pain.
To understand behavior, one must ask:
What emotion is allowed here?
What emotion is forbidden?
Who may express anger?
Who must remain pleasant?
Who may cry?
Who must stay controlled?
Who is believed when emotional?
Who is discredited?
Emotional acceptability is one of the deepest forms of norm power.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.16 Norms and Directness
Directness is one of the most common sources of norm conflict.
Some fields value direct speech.
They associate directness with clarity, honesty, efficiency, courage, and respect for time.
Other fields value indirect speech.
They associate indirectness with politeness, face protection, maturity, restraint, and relational awareness.
Neither style is universally superior.
Directness can clarify, but it can also humiliate.
Indirectness can protect dignity, but it can also create confusion or avoidance.
A person from a directness norm may see indirect people as evasive, weak, or dishonest.
A person from an indirectness norm may see direct people as rude, aggressive, or socially crude.
The conflict is not only personality. It is norm collision.
The skilled person asks:
Does this field reward directness or indirectness?
Is the relationship safe enough for direct speech?
Is face at stake?
Is clarity urgent?
Is ambiguity creating harm?
Would indirectness protect dignity or hide responsibility?
Would directness serve truth or create unnecessary damage?
Directness is not only a communication style. It is a situational choice.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.17 Norms and Privacy
Privacy norms define what may be asked, revealed, recorded, shared, or hidden.
Different fields have different privacy boundaries.
A doctor may ask questions that would be invasive from a stranger.
A close friend may ask about feelings that would be inappropriate from a colleague.
A family may expect access to personal decisions that an individual sees as private.
A workplace may require information that feels personal.
A public platform may turn private life into content.
A romantic relationship may require disclosure, but not unlimited access.
Privacy norms often produce conflict because people disagree about where the boundary lies.
One person says, “I’m just concerned.”
Another says, “You’re invading my life.”
One person says, “We are family; we should know.”
Another says, “This is my decision.”
One person says, “Transparency builds trust.”
Another says, “I still need boundaries.”
Privacy is not only about secrecy. It is about control over exposure.
Situational intelligence asks:
What does this field have a legitimate right to know?
What belongs to the person?
What belongs to the relationship?
What belongs to the institution?
What becomes dangerous if revealed?
What becomes distrustful if hidden?
Privacy norms define the boundary between connection and intrusion.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.18 Norms and Time
Situations also contain time norms.
Time norms define punctuality, response speed, waiting, urgency, duration, frequency, and acceptable delay.
In some fields, being five minutes late is normal.
In others, it is disrespectful.
In some relationships, replying after a day is acceptable.
In others, it signals distance.
In some workplaces, fast response is expected.
In others, deep work requires delayed response.
In some cultures, time is strict and scheduled.
In others, time is relational and flexible.
Time norms influence interpretation.
A delayed reply may mean busyness, avoidance, disrespect, loss of interest, careful thought, or simply a different response norm.
A long meeting may mean seriousness in one institution and inefficiency in another.
A short answer may mean clarity in one field and coldness in another.
A quick decision may mean decisiveness in one setting and recklessness in another.
Time is not merely technical. It is social.
People express respect, priority, power, and care through time.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.19 Norms and Body
Bodily behavior is also norm-governed.
Distance, touch, posture, eye contact, clothing, gesture, facial expression, eating, movement, and bodily exposure are interpreted through norms.
A hug may be warmth in one field and violation in another.
Standing close may signal intimacy in one culture and intrusion in another.
Looking down may signal respect in one field and insecurity in another.
Relaxed posture may signal confidence in one setting and disrespect in another.
Formal dress may signal seriousness in one institution and stiffness in another.
Eating loudly, sitting position, hand gestures, facial expressiveness, and bodily stillness can all be norm-sensitive.
The body speaks inside a field.
People often judge bodily behavior immediately, before conscious reasoning.
This is why cross-cultural and cross-class interaction can produce subtle discomfort. People may not know which norm has been violated, but they feel that something is “off.”
Situational intelligence includes bodily norm awareness.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.20 Norms and Language Register
Every field has expectations about language register.
Register refers to the level and style of language: formal, informal, technical, intimate, bureaucratic, academic, casual, polite, humorous, ceremonial, professional, vulgar, or poetic.
A sentence that fits one register may misfit another.
Technical language may be appropriate in a professional meeting but alienating in family conversation.
Casual slang may be bonding among friends but inappropriate in a court document.
Emotional language may be necessary in intimacy but excessive in a procedural report.
Bureaucratic language may be required by institutions but feel cold in a personal apology.
Academic language may demonstrate rigor in university but sound pretentious in ordinary conversation.
A skilled communicator does not only know what to say. They know what register the field requires.
Register fit is a core part of acceptability.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.21 Norm Conflict
Norm conflict occurs when two or more norm systems collide.
This may happen across cultures, generations, classes, professions, families, genders, platforms, or institutions.
A young person may value personal boundaries, while parents value family access.
An engineer may value technical precision, while a manager values stakeholder alignment.
A doctor may value procedure, while a patient wants emotional recognition.
A Western-trained professional may value direct feedback, while a local team values face protection.
An online community may reward expressive intensity, while an offline institution expects restraint.
A romantic partner may value constant communication, while the other values autonomy.
Norm conflict is often misread as character conflict.
One side says, “You are rude.”
The other says, “You are unclear.”
One says, “You are cold.”
The other says, “You are too emotional.”
One says, “You are controlling.”
The other says, “You are irresponsible.”
One says, “You are fake.”
The other says, “You lack manners.”
Often, both are interpreting through different norm systems.
The first task is not to decide who is bad. The first task is to identify which norms are colliding.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.22 Norm Negotiation
When people do not share norms, they must negotiate them.
Norm negotiation means making expectations explicit, adjusting behavior, setting boundaries, and creating a workable shared field.
This may involve saying:
“In this team, direct disagreement is acceptable, but personal attacks are not.”
“In this relationship, I need privacy around some decisions, even if I care about you.”
“In this meeting, let’s separate brainstorming from decision-making.”
“In this family conversation, I’m willing to discuss my plans, but not through comparison or humiliation.”
“In this group chat, sensitive topics should not be screenshotted or forwarded.”
“In this collaboration, late responses are fine, but urgent issues need a separate channel.”
Norm negotiation turns hidden expectations into explicit agreements.
It prevents people from assuming that their own norm is universal.
It also allows fields to evolve.
Without norm negotiation, people rely on guessing, resentment, pressure, and punishment.
With norm negotiation, interaction becomes more conscious.
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
section: 6.23 Norms Can Be Healthy or Harmful
text:
6.23 Norms Can Be Healthy or Harmful
Not all norms are equal.
Some norms protect dignity, safety, fairness, clarity, and trust.
For example:
Do not humiliate people publicly.
Do not share private information without consent.
Let others finish speaking.
Give credit for others’ work.
Respect physical boundaries.
Apologize when you cause harm.
Clarify expectations in high-stakes situations.
Do not exploit vulnerability.
These norms make interaction safer and more humane.
Other norms protect hierarchy, control, silence, shame, exclusion, or false harmony.
For example:
Never question elders.
Never challenge leaders.
Never admit weakness.
Always keep family matters hidden.
Always appear successful.
Do not discuss unfairness.
Do not make powerful people uncomfortable.
Sacrifice yourself to preserve harmony.
These norms may produce order, but they can also damage people.
Therefore, norm awareness must include norm evaluation.
The question is not only:
What is the norm here?
The question is also:
What does this norm do to people?
crumbs: Part II — Norms, Scripts, and Culture

title: 6  Norms and Acceptability
text:
6.24 Norms and Moral Disguise
Some norms present themselves as morality while hiding social control.
A group may call obedience “respect.”
It may call silence “maturity.”
It may call conformity “professionalism.”
It may call self-erasure “sacrifice.”
It may call fear “prudence.”
